title: Bond enthalpies
examples: How do I use bond enthalpies to predict if a reaction will happen?
Is bond enthalpy the same as bond energy?
What are the units I should expect for bond enthalpies?

explain.say: Today we are learning about bond enthalpies in chemistry.

items: Bonds are the connections between atoms.

explain.say: When we break bonds, we must put energy into the system.
When new bonds form, energy is released back into the surroundings.
The overall change in enthalpy is bonds broken minus bonds made.
For example, breaking two C-H bonds requires a certain amount of energy.
If we form three new C-H bonds, energy is released.

faq.q: What are bond enthalpies measured in?
faq.a: They are typically measured in units of kilojoules per mole, or kJ per mole.
asks: What are the units for bond enthalpy?
Do I use kJ or J for this calculation?

faq.q: Can I use bond enthalpies for reactions in water?
faq.a: Bond enthalpies give an estimate for the energy change, but they do not account for the solvent effects in water.
asks: Does the solvent matter for this calculation?
Is this calculation accurate for aqueous solutions?

faq.q: Why do I subtract the formed energy from the broken energy?
faq.a: We subtract because breaking bonds is positive energy input, and forming bonds is negative energy output.
asks: Should I add or subtract the numbers?
How does the sign of the overall energy change?

faq.q: Do I use the average bond enthalpy or the specific one?
faq.a: You should use the average bond enthalpy value given in the problem unless the specific bond type is provided.
asks: Which bond value should I select?
Is there a difference between average and specific?

faq.q: What does a positive value for ΔH mean?
faq.a: A positive value for the overall enthalpy change means energy was absorbed, making the reaction endothermic.
asks: If ΔH is positive, what happens to the energy?
Does a positive number mean heat is taken in?

facts: Bond enthalpy is the energy required to break one mole of a specific bond in the gaseous state.
Breaking bonds always requires an input of energy, making this process endothermic.
Forming bonds always releases energy, making this process exothermic.
The calculation involves: Bonds Broken (Energy Input) minus Bonds Formed (Energy Released).

quiz.say: Consider the reaction: $\text{A} + \text{B} \rightarrow \text{AB}$. If the energy to break the bonds in A and B is $400 \text{ kJ/mol}$, and the energy to form the A-B bond is $150 \text{ kJ/mol}$, what is the overall enthalpy change?
quiz.why: You subtract the energy released when forming the bond from the energy needed to break the initial bonds. A positive result means energy was absorbed.

wrong.0: Adding the two values incorrectly treats both processes as energy inputs.
wrong.1: Treating the energy released as a subtraction from the initial energy is incorrect.
wrong.2: Only considering the energy released ignores the energy needed to start the reaction.

quiz.say: Which statement correctly describes the energy changes when using bond enthalpies?
quiz.show: Breaking = Energy In; Forming = Energy Out

options.show: The energy released is always added to the broken energy.
options.say: The energy released is always added to the broken energy.

options.show: The calculation only requires knowing the final bonds formed.
options.say: The calculation only requires knowing the final bonds formed.

options.show: Energy to break bonds is added, and energy released upon forming bonds is subtra
options.say: Energy to break bonds is added, and energy released upon forming bonds is subtra

options.show: Both breaking and forming are always energy inputs.
options.say: Both breaking and forming are always energy inputs.

quiz.why: The formula is structured as: $\Delta H = \sum \text{Energy}{\text{broken}} - \sum \text{Energy}{\text{formed}}$.

wrong.0: The energy released is subtracted because it reduces the overall energy change.
wrong.1: You must account for both the bonds that break and the bonds that form.
wrong.3: Forming bonds releases energy, which is an energy output, not an input.

quiz.say: A reaction requires breaking three C-H bonds and forming two C-H bonds. If the bond enthalpy for C-H is $413 \text{ kJ/mol}$, what is the enthalpy change?

wrong.1: This only calculates the energy required to break the bonds, ignoring the bonds formed.
wrong.2: This incorrectly adds the energy values together instead of subtracting.
